name: Intentionality bias
statement: Faced with an action that could have been done on purpose or by accident, people lean towards on purpose, and deciding it was an accident is held to be the slower step.
meaning: Two claims travel together and have separate evidence. The first is a pattern in the data: when an action is genuinely ambiguous, more than half of judgements come back intentional. The second is a process story, Evelyn Rosset's dual-process model, in which the intentional reading is the automatic default and the unintentional reading arrives only when higher-level processing overrides it. The first claim is a proportion. The second predicts that anything which starves the slower process, time pressure, cognitive load, alcohol, should push the proportion up. Three neighbouring entries cover different things. The side-effect effect holds the actor's mental state fixed and varies whether the outcome is good or bad. Agent detection asks whether an agent is there at all, not what the agent meant. Hostile attribution bias is about reading hostile intent in particular, and about who does it, namely aggressive people. Intentionality bias is the broader claim that the intentional reading wins by default for everyone.

origin.note: Rosset's paper reports three studies. Participants read sentences describing actions that could be done on purpose or by accident, such as 'He set the house on fire', and chose an interpretation. Half judged under speeded conditions, and that group judged more sentences intentional. A second study collected free descriptions and found more intentional readings even for prototypically accidental actions. A third found that people asked to sort sentences as intentional or unintentional later remembered more of the unintentional ones than a control group sorting sentences as pleasant or unpleasant. The article is closed access and no open copy was found, so the abstract is all that was read for this entry.

evidence:
Two later teams rebuilt the task without sentences, which matters because Rosset noted that wording alone might invite intentional readings. Moore and Pope showed 35 undergraduates 24 clips of a hand with a finger strapped into a key. Participants were told the movements would be a mixture of active presses and passive pulls by a pulley under the keyboard. Every clip was in fact the same passive pull. They called 64.2% of them intentional, SD 17.6, t(34) = 4.76, p < .001 against a test value of 50, and the score rose with schizotypy on both the Cardiff Anomalous Perceptions Scale, r = .534, p = .001, and the Peters Delusion Inventory, r = .451, p = .006. A later study using the same apparatus and the same perceptions scale found no overall correlation, and it is described under replication.

Slavny and Moore ran Rosset's sentences online on 59 people at the timing of his unspeeded condition. Intentional judgements ran at 65.95%, SD 23.00, for neutral and prototypically intentional sentences and 20.12%, SD 11.87, for prototypically accidental ones. Self-reported cognitive empathy predicted the accidental-sentence score, F(2,56) = 5.06, p = .010, R² = .15, carried by perspective taking, and affective empathy did not.

The drinking study is the strongest support for the process claim. Bègue, Bushman, Giancola, Subra and Rosset used a balanced placebo design in a field experiment disguised as a food tasting, with a target blood alcohol content of 0.10%, and report that intoxicated people read more acts as intentional than sober people did. Their abstract was read; the article was not opened, and no figures from it appear here.

examples.tag: The shoulder in a narrow corridor
examples.text: Knocked as somebody passes, a man's first reading is that it was meant. The thought that the corridor is simply too narrow for two arrives second, and has to be reached for rather than supplied.
A text that goes a day without a reply is read as a decision not to answer rather than as a phone left at the bottom of a bag. Both readings fit what happened, and only one of them comes first.

A door closes as a visitor reaches the porch, and she takes it as a slight. Ambiguity is what the claim needs: where an act is plainly an accident, most people say so, and the proportion is nothing like fixed.

replication.headline: Endorsement sits above chance in three samples of the video task, a fourth shows it tracking the actor's posture, and speeding and memory load moved nothing.
replication.detail:
Hughes, Sandry and Trafimow tested the speeded manipulation directly and report that participants were no more likely to judge ambiguous actions intentional when speeded than when unspeeded. They also report that people responded faster and more consistently to unintentional actions, which runs against the claim that the unintentional reading is the effortful one. Their abstract was read; the article is closed access and its sample size could not be obtained.

Eisenkoeck, de Fockert and Moore substituted working memory load for time pressure, on the reasoning that load isolates the resource a Type 2 process is supposed to need. In a laboratory experiment of 42 people split across no, low and high load, load did nothing, F(2,38) = 0.114, p = .892, η² = 0.006. An online experiment of 323 people gave the same answer, F(2) = 1.49, p = .227, η² = 0.009. Working memory capacity did not predict endorsement in the online sample either, r = -.088, p = .057.

What did hold in both experiments was the proportion. Endorsement averaged 62.5%, SD 16, in the laboratory, t(41) = 5.065, p < .001, d = 0.782, and 61.12%, SD 19.75, online, t(322) = 10.12, p < .001, d = 0.563. The d in the structured field is that second figure. It measures the distance between observed endorsement and a 50% midpoint on Moore and Pope's video task, not a repeat of Rosset's speeded comparison, for which no effect size was obtainable. The authors conclude that their results undermine the dual-process model and call it incomplete.

Tidoni and six colleagues rebuilt the same video task and found that the proportion is not one number. Two actors were filmed with the index finger bent over the button or held straight, and every movement was again made by the hidden device. In 41 people the posture settled the judgement, chi-square(1) = 54.89, p < .001. Bent-finger clips were called intentional on 0.716 of trials in the first block and 0.626 in the second. Straight-finger clips were called intentional on 0.252 and 0.286. Onset delay had no main effect on the judgement, chi-square(5) = 4.91, p = .427. Total scores on the Cardiff Anomalous Perceptions Scale did not correlate with attribution overall, r = -.044, p = .789 among the 40 people with complete scales, and the two postures gave correlations of opposite sign. The authors conclude that intentionality attribution is not based on processes that automatically infer intentions as the primary cause of human actions.

study.cite: Eisenkoeck, A. E., de Fockert, J. W., & Moore, J. W. (2024). Investigating the effect of cognitive load on the intentionality bias. Psychological Research, 89(1), 4.

limits:
Rosset's own numbers are not in this entry because they could not be read. Elsevier answered with a bot challenge rather than a paywall page on 21 September 2026, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar each record the article closed with no open location. Figures for the speeded and unspeeded groups circulate on index pages and in search summaries, and none of them was traced to a document, so they are left out.

The evidence base is small and narrow. The video paradigm has been run on 35, 41, 42 and 323 people, the sentence paradigm on 59 in the individual-differences study, and the three named tests of the process claim used speeding, alcohol and working memory load rather than the same manipulation twice. Eisenkoeck and colleagues note that their stimulus is a finger on a key and may lack the agentic properties Rosset's hypothesis assumed.

The benchmark deserves scrutiny. In the video task the comparison is against 50%, which is the chance rate of a two-alternative forced choice, and participants were told the clips were a mixture when in fact all of them were passive. That design makes the endorsement figure a genuine error rate. It also means the reported effect size describes a departure from a midpoint rather than a difference between conditions.

Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, OpenAIRE, CORE and Unpaywall on 21 September 2026. No meta-analysis, registered replication report or multi-site project on the intentionality bias was located. One paper remains unread. Willard and Foster published a high-powered replication and extension of Slavny and Moore in Personality and Individual Differences in 2026. Crossref verifies the citation and deposits no abstract for it, PubMed and Europe PMC hold no record, and ScienceDirect answered with a bot challenge, so nothing is said here about what it found.
misreadings:
The commonest error is to treat the proportion as proof of the process. People call an ambiguous finger movement intentional about 62% of the time in three samples, but that figure is not a constant. When Tidoni and colleagues varied the actor's posture the same task gave about 0.7 for one posture and about 0.25 for the other. The sentence task splits the same way, since Slavny and Moore recorded 65.95% on neutral and prototypically intentional sentences and 20.12% on prototypically accidental ones. That people judge as they do because an automatic mechanism proposes intention first is a separate claim, and the two manipulations built to test it, speeding and working memory load, produced nothing.

The second error is to fold in the Knobe effect. That effect varies the moral valence of a foreseen side effect and keeps the actor's mental state constant; this one varies nothing and asks what an ambiguous act was. A result about blame leaking into intentionality judgements is not a result about a default setting.

The third concerns children. Rosset and Rottman argue that the developmental record shows over-attribution rather than immaturity, citing Smith's 1978 study in which four-year-olds rated sneezing and chewing as equally wanted and intended, with five-year-olds better and only six-year-olds matching adults. Their reading is that six-year-olds have not learnt that chewing is intentional but that sneezing is not. That is a reinterpretation of older data offered in a theoretical paper, not a new experiment, and Smith's paper was not opened for this entry. Rosset and Rottman also cite Shultz, Wells and Sarda, Lang and Perner, and Montgomery and Lightner for three- and four-year-olds claiming they intended their own knee-jerk reflexes and guided hand movements. Those studies are named on their authority.

A fourth is to read the schizotypy correlation as a clinical finding. Moore and Pope tested 35 healthy undergraduates on questionnaires of delusional ideation and anomalous perception. Nobody with a diagnosis was in the sample. Tidoni and colleagues later gave the same perceptions scale to 40 people on the same apparatus, found no overall correlation, and found the sign reversing between the two postures.
